slides: Okay, a quick summary before you practice.
The big ideas of geometric understanding... with almost no calculation.
The circle is the most efficient shape. Think of the country rule: the most land, the least border.
So read what's fixed. The perimeter, or the area.
With rectangles, the closer to a square, the more area. And with regular polygons, the more sides, the more like a circle.
Move the vertex straight away from the segment, and the angle closes. Bring it closer, and it opens toward a hundred and eighty.
Now keep the vertex, and stretch the segment. The old angle sits inside the new one. So it's bigger.
And the farther the vertex is from an arc, the smaller the angle.
An angle lying on a diameter. With the vertex on the circle, it's exactly ninety.
Inside the circle, the vertex is closer. So the angle opens... more than ninety.
Outside, it's farther. So the angle closes, less than ninety.
Two rods that don't change, and the angle between them opens. Well, the third side always gets longer.
But the area is different. It grows only up to ninety degrees. At ninety, it's the greatest.
And here's the trap. Forty and a hundred and forty degrees give the same height... so the same area.
The anchor you'll use most is the right angle. So compare with Pythagoras.
The longest side is longer than in the right triangle? Then it's obtuse. Shorter? Acute.
And always use the longest side as c.

One allowed case where a claim fails, and "must be true" is out.
The figure isn't necessarily drawn to scale. So trust the givens, not the picture.
Exaggerate. Push the free point to the end, then put it in the middle.
"It cannot be determined"? Only if you can draw two figures that keep every given, and give two different answers.
In geometry, it's almost never the answer. So if you can't build the two figures, find the reason the answer is fixed.
The apex slides along a line parallel to the base. The height stays the same. So the area stays the same.
But the perimeter changes. And you'll see this in a trapezoid too.
Okay, before you practice, ask yourself these questions.
The traps: trusting the drawing, and thinking a wider angle always means a bigger area.
